extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians proposing focused AIM workshops; prospective workshop organizers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for preparing and submitting proposals to run a focused 5-day American Institute of Mathematics (AIM) workshop (in‑person or virtual). Covers required content, participant lists, scope, logistics, selection, and scheduling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Description of the workshop’s motivation, focus and goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals should include a description of the workshop’s motivation, focus and goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most workshop proposals are around 3 pages long because that is enough space to describe the motivation, focus, and goals. Emphasis should be placed on the timeliness of the topic and the anticipated outcomes resulting from this workshop. Special attention should be given to describing how the proposed focused workshop is the appropriate venue for achieving the desired outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discussion of the mathematics involved
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals should include a discussion of the mathematics involved in the workshop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide sufficient mathematical detail to convey the specific mathematical goal that will form the focus of the workshop. The AIM staff can help refine the focus if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: List of organizers (at least 2, at most 4)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals should include a list of organizers (at least 2, at most 4).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organizers are responsible for the scientific aspects of the workshop: refining the focus, discussing participant selection, and scheduling activities. AIM staff handle logistics (invitations, registration, travel, accommodations, advertising, and applicant solicitation).

rubrics_metrics.name: List of potential participants
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals should include a list of potential participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For a typical workshop with 28 participants, list 15–20 potential participants. If you can easily list 30 potential participants, that likely indicates the mathematical goals are too broad. A list of 50 whose contributions would be vital indicates the scope is too broad. You do not need to contact potential participants before submitting; the list is to help the AIM Scientific Board evaluate scope. The list is not binding and may change in response to Board recommendations; organizers propose an initial list containing three quarters of the participants, and the remaining quarter is selected from open applications.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematics subject classification and references
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals should include the mathematics subject classification and a list of references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide appropriate MSC codes and references to situate the workshop within the literature and to clarify the technical background for reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposal length and formatting guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: How long and how to format the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most proposals are around 2–3 (commonly 3) pages. There is no formal page limit, but do not use typographic tricks to fit content into a given number of pages. Use sufficient space to describe motivation, focus, goals, and the mathematics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate scope — focused rather than broad
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals must define a focused topic appropriate for an AIM workshop rather than a broad conference topic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AIM workshops are focused in nature; broad topics suitable for a large conference are not appropriate. Use participant-list size as an indicator of scope. AIM staff can work with proposers to narrow a topic.

rubrics_metrics.name: In‑person vs virtual format rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposal must specify whether the workshop is in-person or virtual, and each topic should be proposed for only one format.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is possible to submit multiple proposals on different topics, but each topic should either be for an in-person workshop or a virtual workshop, but not both. Read AIM style of workshops and AIM virtual workshops guidance before submitting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant number limits and flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Maximum workshop size is 28 participants; fewer participants are allowed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The upper limit of 28 is set by the focused nature of AIM workshops and facilities. Fewer than 28 is permissible. Typical planning assumes 28, but propose accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overseas participant limit
rubrics_metrics.description: Participation by overseas participants is typically limited to 25%.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan participant composition with this guideline in mind; exceptions are not guaranteed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Funding coverage — no external funding required
rubrics_metrics.description: No external funding is necessary: AIM provides funding for invited workshop participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: AIM provides travel allowance, hotel accommodations, and a per diem for meals for invited participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission deadline and selection body
rubrics_metrics.description: Most workshops are selected from proposals received by the annual November 1 deadline; workshops are selected by the AIM Scientific Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contact AIM staff for details about exceptions or late/emerging-topic proposals; due to funding shortfalls there may be years when new workshop proposals cannot be accepted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scheduling expectations for virtual vs in‑person
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical scheduling expectations differ for virtual and in-person workshops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Successful virtual workshop proposals from the November 1 deadline can often be scheduled any week next year (except holidays). A few successful in-person proposals can take place the next calendar year, but most will meet in the following year. Virtual workshops can be scheduled more quickly and have a smaller carbon footprint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participant selection process and bindingness of initial list
rubrics_metrics.description: Organizers propose an initial participant list containing three quarters of participants; the remaining quarter is selected from open applications. The initial list is not binding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The initial list helps the AIM Scientific Board evaluate scope; prior to scheduling, organizers will work with AIM staff to refine focus and modify the invitation list as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expected workshop daily structure and presentations
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical workshop day consists of two talks in the morning and discussion sessions or smaller working groups in the afternoon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While all participants will be fully funded, most participants will not give a formal presentation. Emphasis is on discussion and collaborative work rather than many formal talks (fewer talks than a typical conference).

rubrics_metrics.name: AIM staff assistance in proposal preparation
rubrics_metrics.description: AIM staff are available to assist in the preparation of workshop proposals and to work with potential organizers to define or narrow focus.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For further details or assistance, contact workshops@aimath.org or any of the AIM staff. The staff also handle logistical tasks (invitations, registration, travel/accommodation arrangements, advertising, and solicitation of applicants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Late or emerging-topic proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Some places are reserved to allow workshops on topics of emerging interest to be organized in a timely manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you miss the November 1 deadline, contact AIM staff for details about reserved slots for timely/emerging topics.
